Another beginner might average all ethical rules with fixed weights. That also fails because the right balance may depend on observed outcomes. Fixed weights cannot adapt when one ethical lens becomes more relevant under the evidence the system is seeing.
308.ap: The paper's central move is to fold moral uncertainty into the bandit choice itself. It starts from the Upper Confidence Bound idea: favor actions that have done well, but also give a temporary bonus to actions whose value is still uncertain because they have been tried less. The extension is that an action's value is not treated as one plain reward number. It is judged through competing ethical frameworks, and those frameworks receive dynamic moral weights. In concrete terms, the learner keeps track of evidence from outcomes and uses that evidence to adjust how much each moral lens contributes to the action score. The system can therefore explore uncertain actions, use actions that already look good, and revise the moral mixture as experience arrives. The abstract also says the authors derive upper limits of regret, so the method is meant to preserve a disciplined bound on how much is lost while learning.
308.mech: The mechanism begins with a set of possible actions, the bandit arms. At each round, the system must choose one arm before it knows the next outcome. For each arm, it keeps evidence from past pulls: what happened when that action was chosen and how those outcomes looked under the ethical frameworks being considered. A standard UCB score has two pieces. One piece is the current estimated value of an arm, built from past observations. The other is an uncertainty allowance, larger for arms that have not been tried much, so the system does not prematurely settle on a lucky early winner. This paper adds a moral layer to the estimated value. Instead of scoring an outcome through only one ethical rule, it evaluates the competing moral frameworks and combines them using weights that can change over time. After an action is chosen and an outcome is observed, the learner updates both its evidence about that action and the moral-weighted score used in future choices. The next choice is then made by comparing the updated UCB-style scores across arms. What comes out is a policy, meaning a rule for selecting the next action from the current evidence, that balances performance, exploration, and changing ethical priorities.
308.math: The first mathematical object is a repeated decision problem under uncertainty. Each arm has an unknown value, and the learner only sees the value of the arm it actually chooses. Probability is the language for the unknown outcome: repeated observations slowly turn guesswork into an estimate, while sparse observations must remain visibly uncertain. Upper Confidence Bound adds a cautious optimism rule. In plain terms, it says an arm should look attractive either because it has earned good outcomes or because the learner has too little evidence to rule it out. That creates the exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff: learn about uncertain arms without wasting too many decisions away from arms that already look strong. This paper adds weighted moral scoring. A weight is a dial saying how much one ethical framework contributes to the current action value. Dynamic weights mean those dials are updated as outcomes arrive instead of being frozen at the start. Regret is another key idea: it measures the accumulated gap between what the learner did and what a better-informed chooser would have done under the target scoring rule. An upper regret limit is a promise about how badly the learning process can fall behind. The central tradeoff is performance versus ethical pluralism: the system must remain effective while not pretending that one moral rule was certain from the beginning.
308.dots: This paper sits next to the conference's recurring work on probability, choosing actions by feedback, and responsible AI. It is close to reinforcement-learning and bandit papers because the learner acts, observes, and adjusts rather than only labeling stored data. It is also close to advertising allocation and recommendation exploration, where a system must choose among options while avoiding the trap of always showing the current favorite. The difference is that this paper makes the score itself morally uncertain. That connects it to fairness and responsible decision-making work: many systems must decide who receives visibility, service, risk, or protection while historical data and human goals disagree. It also touches optimization, in the plain sense of defining what counts as a bad choice and searching for choices that reduce that badness. Here, defining badness is part of the problem, because competing ethical frameworks may score the same outcome differently.
308.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it keeps uncertainty visible in two places where a fixed rule hides it. First, the UCB part keeps ordinary outcome uncertainty visible. An action that has not been tried much is not dismissed just because its first few results were weak or because another action was lucky early. That helps the system discover options whose value would otherwise remain unseen. Second, the dynamic moral weights keep ethical uncertainty visible. Instead of pretending that the designer already knows the single correct moral rule, the learner carries competing frameworks into the decision score and lets their influence adapt as outcomes are observed. This is useful when the environment reveals tensions that were not clear at design time. The regret analysis matters because flexible ethical weighting could otherwise sound unconstrained: the system might chase changing values without any learning discipline. By extending UCB rather than replacing it with loose judgment, the paper aims to retain a measurable limit on learning cost while adding moral flexibility.
308.po: The payoff is a decision rule for settings where learning from outcomes is necessary but plain reward maximization is too narrow. According to the abstract, the algorithm balances ethical considerations and performance under different levels of moral uncertainty. It gives a bandit system a way to adapt when competing moral frameworks, such as total-benefit reasoning and duty-based reasoning, both have a claim on the choice. The reported theoretical regret limits also make the contribution more than a verbal ethics layer: the authors aim to show that the learner can stay bounded in how much it loses while exploring actions and moral weights.
308.limits: The abstract does not say how the moral weights are initialized, what outcome information is needed to update them, or who decides which ethical frameworks are included. Those choices matter because a missing moral lens cannot receive weight later. The approach also assumes that outcomes can be evaluated under the competing frameworks in a form the bandit can use. Real ethical disagreement may be harder to reduce to comparable scores. The regret guarantee depends on the formal setup used in the paper, so it may not cover changing populations, strategic users, bad measurements, or harms that appear long after the observed reward. The abstract supports moral flexibility, not proof of universal ethical correctness.

309.bp: A search system often has to find the right document without reading every document in full at answer time. One practical shortcut is to store a shorter version of each document, then search over those summaries. That saves space and may make the important parts easier to compare with a user's query. But a summary written to sound fluent is not automatically a good search object. It may omit the exact clue that would make the document retrievable, or it may use wording that no longer matches the way the retriever learned to compare queries and full documents. ReSuMe serves this pressure point. It treats summarization and retrieval as two parts of one machine: the summarizer must produce document shortcuts that help search, and the retriever must learn how to search those shortcuts. The goal is not merely nicer summaries, but summaries that preserve the evidence a dense retriever needs to rank documents.
309.wh: The hard part is that the retriever and the summarizer can silently disagree about what a document is. A dense retriever is a model that turns a query and each document into comparable numeric descriptions, then ranks documents by closeness. If it was trained on full documents, its sense of closeness is shaped by full-document wording, length, and detail. At inference time, ReSuMe's setting asks that retriever to operate on synthetic summaries instead. That creates a distribution shift, meaning the material seen at use time has a different shape from the material seen during training. A readable summary can still be a bad retrieval target if it drops rare facts, changes wording, or compresses several ideas into vague language. The central tension is compression versus findability: summaries should be short, but search needs the specific traces that distinguish one relevant document from many plausible neighbors.
309.naive: A smart beginner would build the system in two separate steps. First, train or choose a summarizer that writes high-quality document summaries. Second, give those summaries to an existing dense retriever and expect search to become cheaper and perhaps cleaner. This fails because linguistic quality and retrieval usefulness are not the same objective. A summary can be grammatical, concise, and faithful while still removing the phrase, entity, or detail that would match a query. The retriever also has no reason to understand the summarizer's preferred style if it learned from full documents. The pipeline breaks at the boundary between the two models: each component looks reasonable alone, but the pair is not trained to agree.
309.ap: ReSuMe's core idea is to make the summarizer and retriever adapt to each other instead of freezing one side and hoping the other side fits. The language model is trained to generate summaries whose value is judged by retrieval relevance, not by wording quality alone. At the same time, the retrieval model is updated on those generated summaries so it learns the new kind of document representation it will actually face. The process alternates: improve the summarizer using feedback from retrieval, then improve the retriever using the summaries the current summarizer produces. In concrete terms, the paper turns summarization into a search-serving action. A summary is good when it helps a relevant document rise in the ranked list for the right query. The repeated back-and-forth is meant to reduce the gap between full-document training and summary-based inference.
309.mech: The mechanism begins with documents, queries, and a dense retrieval system such as Contriever. The summarizer first produces synthetic summaries of documents. These summaries are not treated as final products judged only by human-like readability. They become the objects that the retriever must search. Next, the language model behind the summarizer is fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement-learning procedure where several candidate outputs can be compared as a group and the model is pushed toward outputs that receive better reward. Here the reward is tied to retrieval relevance: a summary is favored when using it helps the retriever place the right document higher. Then the retriever is updated on the generated summaries using contrastive learning, which means learning by pulling matching query-summary pairs closer and pushing mismatched pairs farther apart in the retriever's comparison space. After that retriever update, the summarizer faces a changed search partner, so the process can repeat. Each phase changes the environment for the other phase: better summaries give the retriever cleaner training material, and a retriever adapted to those summaries gives more meaningful feedback to the summarizer. The output is a pair of models, one producing retrieval-oriented summaries and one searching those summaries more effectively.
309.math: The main mathematical ideas are scoring, comparison, and alternating optimization. Scoring means deciding what counts as a better summary. ReSuMe does not make fluency the only score; it uses retrieval relevance, so the score asks whether the summary helps a query find the correct document. Comparison appears inside dense retrieval: query text and summary text are converted into numeric descriptions, and closeness between those descriptions becomes the basis for ranking. This is a useful compression of meaning, but it is also lossy: many document details must be squeezed into a limited numeric form, so the system must learn which details matter for search. Reinforcement learning enters as trial-and-feedback learning for the summarizer. The model tries different summary wordings and is rewarded when they improve retrieval behavior. Group Relative Policy Optimization, as named in the abstract, adds relative comparison among candidate outputs rather than judging each output in isolation. Contrastive learning is the retriever's matching math: make true query-summary pairs closer than false pairs. The alternating structure matters because each side changes the data seen by the other. The tradeoff is compression versus discriminative detail, with training pressure used to keep shortened text searchable.
309.dots: This paper sits in the repo's information-retrieval and search family because its basic object is a ranked list: from a large document collection, show the documents most likely to answer a query. It also neighbors the retrieval-augmented generation family, where many papers ask whether the information fed into a language model is actually useful rather than merely related. ReSuMe is upstream of that concern: before an answer model reasons over retrieved material, the retriever must first find the right material from compact document surrogates. The paper connects to ranking, similarity, language models, and optimization. Ranking decides which documents get surfaced; similarity decides what counts as close enough; the language model writes the searchable summaries; optimization repeatedly changes model behavior to reduce retrieval errors. Compared with RAG papers that prune evidence chains, handle conflicts, or decide when to retrieve, ReSuMe focuses on making the document representation itself search-ready.
309.ww: The method should work when the main failure is mismatch between the form of stored documents and the form the retriever learned to search. If summaries are created independently, the retriever sees shortened text with different wording and missing detail. ReSuMe attacks that mismatch from both directions. The summarizer receives a reward tied to whether its output helps retrieval, so it has pressure to keep query-relevant identifiers, distinctions, and phrases rather than only writing a pleasant abstract. The retriever then learns from the summaries it will actually compare against queries, so its notion of closeness adapts to compressed document text. Alternation is important because one fixed update is unlikely to solve the problem: as summaries become more retrieval-oriented, the best retriever behavior changes; as the retriever adapts, the feedback given to the summarizer becomes more aligned with the final use case. The abstract's reported gains on MS-MARCO with Contriever suggest that reducing this train-use gap can improve ranked retrieval rather than merely producing shorter documents.
309.po: The payoff is a document summarizer and retriever that are trained as a cooperative pair. Grounded in the abstract, ReSuMe improves retrieval while also producing summaries optimized for retrieval tasks. In experiments with Contriever on MS-MARCO, the paper reports consistent improvements of 13.2 percent in MRR@10, which measures whether highly ranked results put the right answer near the top, and 6.7 percent in Recall@100, which measures whether relevant material appears within the first hundred results. The practical capability is efficient search over synthetic summaries without paying the full penalty of using a retriever trained only on full documents.
309.limits: The abstract supports the general claim but leaves important assumptions open. The approach assumes retrieval relevance is a sufficient training signal for summaries; it may not capture every human need, such as completeness, citation usefulness, or faithful preservation of nuance. It also assumes alternating fine-tuning remains stable and worth its cost for a given deployment. The empirical evidence named in the abstract uses Contriever and MS-MARCO, so the model-agnostic claim still depends on other retrievers, datasets, domains, and summary lengths behaving similarly. The method reduces the gap between full documents and synthetic summaries, but the abstract does not prove that no important facts are lost during summarization.

310.bp: This paper is about a merchant handing part of its selling strategy to an automated agent inside an e-commerce platform. The agent is not only choosing how much to bid for advertising exposure. It is also choosing how much coupon discount to offer on the product. Those two choices are tied together in the real marketplace: a higher bid may bring more shoppers to the product, while a coupon may make those shoppers more likely to buy, but both spend money. The paper matters because marketing management services let merchants delegate these choices, so the platform needs an agent that can act repeatedly without a human rewriting rules each hour. The special pressure is self-funding: the money used for bids and coupons must come from the commission revenue the agent earns. The agent is therefore not spending from a fixed outside budget. It must grow and protect its own fuel while trying to improve business results.
310.wh: The hard part is that the decision is not a single price tag or a single ad bid. It is a sequence of paired choices made in a changing marketplace. If the agent bids high now, it may buy traffic, but that traffic may need a discount to convert into sales. If it discounts too much, sales may rise while commission revenue shrinks, leaving less money for future bids and coupons. If it is too cautious, it may preserve money but miss opportunities. The self-funding constraint makes this sharper than ordinary budget control because spending and future budget are connected through the same sales process. Existing rule-based methods struggle because fixed rules cannot easily adapt when product demand, auction competition, and shopper response change. Existing reinforcement learning methods can also struggle when the delayed consequences of bid and coupon decisions depend on earlier choices in complicated ways. The agent must remember enough history to act, while respecting a constraint that cannot simply be ignored.
310.naive: A smart beginner might separate the problem into two smaller tools: one auto-bidding tool that tries to buy ad traffic cheaply, and one coupon tool that raises or lowers discounts based on recent sales. That is appealing because each tool has an obvious local goal. The bidding tool can chase clicks or exposure, and the coupon tool can chase purchases. The failure is that the two tools spend from the same self-funded pool and influence the same final revenue. A bid that looks good alone may require a costly coupon to produce sales. A coupon that looks good alone may leave too little commission to fund the next advertising round. Treating them separately misses the sequential link between today's spending, today's sales, and tomorrow's available budget.
310.ap: The central move is to treat auto-marketing as one joined sequence-generation problem rather than two disconnected control problems. GAM uses a pre-trained generative model as the starting decision maker, then aligns it after pre-training so its generated action sequences serve the business objective while staying aware of the self-funding constraint. In plain terms, the model proposes sequences of bid and coupon choices. A reward module then judges those choices by two kinds of evidence: whether they help the marketing objective and whether they respect the funding rule. Group Relative Policy Optimization, abbreviated GRPO in the abstract, is the method used to push the model toward better generated choices by comparing candidate behaviors within groups rather than trusting one raw score in isolation. The paper's claim is not merely that a model can output actions; it is that post-training feedback can shape those actions around the specific economics of e-commerce marketing.
310.mech: The mechanism begins with the information available in an e-commerce marketing setting: products, advertising opportunities, possible bids, possible coupon discounts, historical shopper response, and the current state of the agent's self-funded budget. The agent must output a paired decision, not just one number: how much to bid and what coupon discount to offer. Those decisions then affect traffic, purchases, commission revenue, and the money left for later decisions. GAM frames this as a sequence, so each action is read in relation to previous actions and their consequences. First, a pre-trained generative model supplies a general ability to produce structured decisions over time. Second, the model is placed in an offline simulation environment built from a large-scale real-world dataset, according to the abstract, so candidate decision sequences can be evaluated without immediately spending real merchant money. Third, the constraint-aware reward alignment module scores candidate behavior by combining objective gain with constraint satisfaction. A choice that looks profitable but violates the self-funding rule should be pushed down. A choice that earns less immediately but preserves feasible future spending may be judged more favorably. Fourth, GRPO updates the policy, meaning the rule by which the model chooses actions, by comparing groups of generated candidates and strengthening the relatively better ones. The output is an auto-marketing agent tuned to make joint bid-discount decisions under the platform's funding constraint.
310.math: The main mathematical idea is constrained sequential decision making. Sequential means that the answer at one moment changes the situation at the next moment; a bid and coupon today can alter sales, commission revenue, and future spending room. Constrained means that not every high-scoring action is allowed, because the budget for both bids and discounts must come from commission revenue. The problem therefore cannot be solved by simply maximizing sales or clicks. It needs a score that includes both gain and feasibility. The reward alignment module is the paper's way of turning that business rule into a training signal: it says, in measurable terms, which generated action sequences are better and which should be discouraged. Reinforcement learning is used here as repeated adjustment from feedback: the model proposes actions, receives a score, and changes its future behavior toward choices that scored better. GRPO adds a comparison principle. Instead of treating one candidate's reward as an absolute truth, it compares candidates in a group and favors those that are relatively better under the same judging rule. Optimization is the search over possible decision policies: define what counts as success and violation, then adjust the model so the bad parts shrink and the useful parts grow. The key tradeoff is objective maximization versus constraint satisfaction.
310.dots: This paper sits in the advertising and e-commerce family because it tries to choose scarce marketing actions under uncertainty. It is close to auto-bidding papers, but it moves beyond bid control alone by adding coupon discounting as a second action that changes conversion and revenue. It is also close to reinforcement learning work at the conference because the agent learns from scored action sequences rather than from a fixed hand-written rule. The sequence idea matters because the paper's decisions are chained: current spending affects future budget and future room to act. The optimization idea matters because the platform must decide what counts as better when revenue, spending, and constraint satisfaction pull against one another. It also connects to language-model agent work, but the abstract supports a narrow reading: the model is useful because it can generate structured decision sequences and then be aligned with feedback, not because it magically understands commerce. Neighboring e-commerce papers on campaign ranking, budget allocation, bidding, and prediction calibration share the same deeper pressure: automated decisions must serve business goals while respecting operational limits.
310.ww: The approach should improve over the naive split system because it scores the whole marketing move as one coupled action. A bid is not judged only by traffic, and a coupon is not judged only by purchases. Their combined effect is judged against the self-funding rule and the business objective. That matters because the bad decisions in this setting are often locally sensible but globally damaging. Spending more on ads can look good until discounts and commission limits are counted. Discounting more can look good until future marketing fuel is drained. A sequence model can also use history: if earlier actions created enough commission, the next action may safely be more aggressive; if earlier actions strained the budget, the next action must be more careful. GRPO's relative comparison is useful because marketing feedback is noisy. Comparing several candidate sequences under the same reward rule can give a steadier training signal than reacting to one candidate in isolation. The constraint-aware reward gives the model a practical boundary, so learning is aimed at feasible marketing behavior rather than unconstrained short-term gains.
310.po: The payoff is an agent for e-commerce marketing management that can jointly choose advertising bids and product coupon discounts while accounting for the fact that its spending must be funded by its own commission revenue. The abstract says GAM is evaluated in an offline simulation environment built from a large-scale real-world dataset and that experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The capability bought by the method is coordination: bids, discounts, business objectives, and funding constraints are handled in one training loop. For merchants and platforms, that means automated marketing can move from simple bid adjustment toward broader delegated decision making, where the agent chooses multiple linked actions over time.
310.limits: The abstract does not prove how GAM behaves in a live marketplace where competitors, shoppers, and merchants react to the deployed agent. Its evidence is an offline simulation based on a large real-world dataset, so the claim depends on that simulator preserving the important cause-and-effect links among bids, coupons, sales, commission revenue, and future budget. The method also depends on the reward module expressing the right business objective and constraint penalties. If the reward undercounts long-term merchant value, user experience, platform side effects, or rare budget failures, the aligned model may learn the wrong habit. The abstract also does not specify which products, merchants, or market conditions transfer cleanly.

311.bp: Many web companies keep their important operating facts in tables: one row for a user, visit, ad impression, purchase, account, or other event, and many columns describing that event. The job is to predict something useful from those columns, such as a future action or risk. At web scale this is not a neat spreadsheet. The paper describes billions of instances and hundreds of numerical features, each coming from different measurement habits and changing product conditions. KMLP serves the practical need to model such tables without asking experts to hand-design every useful transformation. Before the method name matters, the real problem is this: raw columns rarely speak in the same units, ranges, or shapes, yet a production model must turn them into reliable decisions quickly enough to train on enormous data. The paper proposes a deep tabular model that first reshapes individual features and then learns how reshaped features work together.
311.wh: The difficulty comes from the shape of the columns. The abstract says the features are heterogeneous, anisotropic, heavy-tailed, and non-stationary. In plain terms, different columns behave very differently; some directions in the data matter more than others; rare extreme values may be common enough to distort learning; and the meaning or range of a feature can change over time. A model that treats all columns as ordinary smooth numbers has to spend much of its effort just coping with these uneven shapes. Gradient Boosting Decision Trees are named as strong mainstream models, but the abstract says they face training efficiency and scalability bottlenecks in this setting. The human fallback is manual feature engineering: experts clip values, transform skewed columns, create cross-features, and decide which interactions matter. That can work, but it is slow, dependent on specialized labor, and hard to repeat when the table has hundreds of features and billions of rows.
311.naive: A smart beginner would first feed the raw table into a strong standard model and let the model discover the pattern. If that failed, they would manually clean each troublesome column: rescale large values, bucket strange ranges, smooth extreme tails, and create combinations such as feature A multiplied by feature B. This fails for two reasons. First, the number of possible repairs grows with the number of columns and interactions, so expert work becomes a bottleneck. Second, a fixed hand-written transformation can become stale when the data is non-stationary. The table keeps changing, while the manual recipe reflects yesterday's column behavior. The beginner's approach either asks the model to solve too much at once or asks humans to maintain too many fragile rules.
311.ap: KMLP's central move is to split tabular learning into two jobs. The first job is per-feature repair: a shallow Kolmogorov-Arnold Network sits at the front and learns a custom curve for each input feature. A learnable activation function means the model is not stuck with one fixed way of bending every number; it can learn that one column needs sharp treatment near rare large values while another needs a smoother transformation. The second job is interaction learning: after each column has been reshaped into a more useful representation, a gated Multilayer Perceptron takes over and learns how columns combine. Gating means parts of the model can control which signals pass forward strongly and which are muted. The architecture is hybrid because it does not ask one generic network block to do everything. It first makes individual features easier to read, then captures high-order interactions among the refined features.
311.mech: The mechanism starts with a web-scale table. Each row is an instance, and each instance has hundreds of numerical features from different sources. The KAN front-end receives these raw feature values first. For each feature, it applies a learned nonlinear transformation: instead of merely multiplying the value by a fixed weight, it learns a small adjustable curve that can change how different ranges of that feature are treated. This is the automated substitute for hand-made feature transformations such as clipping, stretching, compressing, or bending a column. The result is a set of refined feature representations, still tied to the original columns but now shaped to make their useful signal easier for the rest of the model to use. These refined values then enter the gMLP backbone. The gMLP mixes information across features and uses gates to decide which combinations should influence later computations. This is where high-order interactions are captured: not only whether feature A matters and feature B matters, but whether their joint pattern matters after both have been reshaped. During training, the whole system is adjusted end to end, so the front-end curves and the interaction backbone are learned together from prediction errors. The output is a predictive model for large dynamic tabular data, evaluated in the paper on public benchmarks and an ultra-large industrial web dataset with billions of samples.
311.math: The first mathematical idea is function learning. A function is a rule that turns an input number into an output number. In this paper, each raw feature needs its own rule because heavy-tailed and uneven columns should not all be treated with the same fixed bend. A Kolmogorov-Arnold Network is used as the front-end because it represents complex multivariable behavior through learnable one-feature transformations that can later be combined. The important everyday idea is decomposition: make a hard many-feature surface easier by first learning useful single-feature curves. The second idea is nonlinear interaction. Nonlinear means that changing a feature can have different effects in different ranges, and high-order interaction means several features together can carry information that no one feature carries alone. The gMLP backbone supplies a learned mixing machine for those refined feature signals. Its gates are mathematical switches with soft settings, not hand-written if-then rules: they let the model score which signals should pass forward for a given example. Training uses error reduction: the model makes predictions, measures how wrong they are, and adjusts the feature curves and mixing weights to reduce that wrongness. The tradeoff is accuracy and adaptivity versus training cost, with KMLP claiming scalability as data grows.
311.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of tabular deep learning, feature engineering, and efficiency. It connects to the broader efficiency/scalability family because its target is not only better prediction but also removing a human and computational bottleneck from industrial-scale modeling. Like retrieval pruning or sparse recommendation systems, it asks which work should be automatic and reusable when the data pile is too large for exhaustive care. It also connects to recurring conference ideas about similarity and ranking indirectly: many web decisions require scoring rows so that items, users, ads, or risks can be sorted or acted on, and those scores depend on turning raw evidence into comparable quantities. A neighboring idea is sequence or time-aware modeling, because the abstract's non-stationarity means the data-generating process changes. KMLP does not present itself as a time-series model, but it addresses one symptom of changing systems: fixed feature recipes become brittle when the columns' behavior drifts.
311.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive approach because it gives the model the right order of chores. Raw heterogeneous features force a standard model to learn useful transformations and cross-feature interactions at the same time. That is like trying to compare people before deciding whether their measurements are in inches, centimeters, logs, or capped ranges. KMLP first learns how each column should be read. If a feature has rare huge values, the learned curve can compress or emphasize ranges in a way that prediction errors reward. If another feature has a smoother relationship with the target, it can receive a different curve. Once each feature is made more legible, the gMLP can spend its capacity on combinations among features rather than on rescuing badly shaped inputs. This also explains why the abstract reports that KMLP's advantage over strong GBDT baselines becomes more pronounced as data scale increases. More data can expose more detailed feature shapes and interactions, while manual engineering and some mainstream models face growing cost and maintenance pressure.
311.po: The payoff is an automated path for web-scale tabular prediction. According to the repo's full abstract, KMLP is tested on multiple public benchmarks and an ultra-large industrial web dataset with billions of samples, and it achieves state-of-the-art performance. The more concrete gain is not the label of state-of-the-art itself; it is that the model can learn feature transformations end to end instead of relying on laborious expert feature engineering. The abstract also claims that its advantage over strong baselines such as GBDTs grows as data scale increases, which is exactly the setting where manual repair and training bottlenecks hurt most.
311.limits: The abstract does not prove that KMLP will work for every table. It assumes that useful signal can be found by first learning per-feature nonlinear transformations and then learning interactions among those transformed features. If the main problem is missing data, label bias, leakage, causal confusion, or sudden feature meaning changes that training data has not seen, this architecture alone may not solve it. The evidence cited is public benchmarks and one ultra-large industrial web dataset, but the abstract does not give details here about tasks, costs, failure cases, or deployment constraints. It also does not show how much interpretability remains after learned feature curves and gated interactions replace human-designed transformations.

312.bp: Machine learning companies offer prediction services over the web (image recognition, medical diagnosis) but users want privacy—they don't want to send raw data to the server. Secure multi-party computation enables a server and user to jointly compute a prediction without the server ever seeing the raw input data, but it's slow and communication-intensive, especially for large models like vision transformers.
312.wh: Vision transformers use attention mechanisms that create highly correlated computations across layers and positions—information needs to flow between distant parts of the model. Naive approaches to secure computation treat each layer the same, not realizing that some layers are communication-heavy while others are compute-heavy. Different layers and positions have different privacy-efficiency trade-offs.
312.ap: SecViT redesigns vision transformers specifically for secure multi-party computation. It analyzes each layer and each position in the model and adapts the attention mechanism to minimize communication under privacy constraints. It adds a 'layer-dependent and load-balancing' attention adapter that reuses features across correlated layers, and develops approximation algorithms for expensive attention and activation operations that preserve accuracy while cutting communication.
312.ww: By analyzing which computations are expensive in the secure setting (communication-heavy), the system can selectively approximate them without harming results. Reusing features across correlated layers reduces redundant secure computation. These optimizations exploit the specific structure of vision transformers rather than applying generic CNN optimizations.
312.po: SecViT reduces communication by 6x and latency by 4.6x compared to prior work while maintaining the same accuracy. This makes private inference over transformers practical for real-world scenarios where users want both privacy and fast predictions.

313.bp: Knowledge is often represented as formal logic rules in ontologies (like OWL, a semantic web standard). To reason over this knowledge, a system must generate proofs—step-by-step logical explanations of why a conclusion follows from the rules. When humans read a proof, they want to understand not just that something is true, but why. Large language models are trained to generate text, but can they generate valid, human-readable logical proofs?
313.wh: Generating proofs is harder than answering questions because a proof must be logically sound (each step must follow from previous premises) and complete (cover all necessary steps). Most work on LLMs focuses on simple reasoning tasks where the model just predicts an answer, not on explaining how it arrived at that answer with formal justification. Logical complexity and formal notation both make this task difficult.
313.ap: This paper builds a dataset and evaluation framework for proof generation in OWL ontologies. It breaks proof generation into sub-tasks: Extraction (find relevant rules), Simplification (make rules easier to understand), and Explanation (convert to natural language). It evaluates a dozen LLMs on these tasks and measures logical completeness (do the proofs actually prove the claim?).
313.ww: By decomposing proof generation into stages, you can identify where models fail. Logical complexity—not fancy notation—is the real blocker: models handle simple chains of reasoning but break on complex proofs. Understanding where models struggle helps identify what makes formal reasoning hard.
313.po: The paper reveals that some models produce strong overall results but fail on complex proofs, that logical structure matters more than notation format, and that noise in input data severely hurts performance. This grounds expectations for what LLMs can and can't do for formal verification and knowledge reasoning tasks.

314.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products, movies, or songs to users based on their past behavior. In practice, popular items (bestsellers, blockbusters) are recommended frequently while niche items rarely appear, even if some users would love them. This 'long-tail' problem means niche item sales and user satisfaction suffer. Large language models are being used as recommenders, but they inherit the same long-tail bias from their training data.
314.wh: An LLM trained on web text and user behavior data has seen millions of mentions of 'Harry Potter' but few mentions of obscure indie films. When recommending, it naturally defaults to the popular items it knows well. Users interested in niche items get frustrated. Naive fine-tuning doesn't fix this because the bias comes partly from the pretraining data (implicit prior) and partly from the recommendation dataset itself (data long-tail).
314.ap: EISAM applies Sharpness-Aware Minimization, a technique from optimization, at the item level. During training, it computes a penalty for each item based on how sharp (locally unstable) the loss landscape is around that item's predictions. Unpopular items tend to have sharper loss landscapes because of limited training examples. EISAM increases the penalty for sharp-loss items, forcing the model to find solutions that work reliably for tail items too.
314.ww: Sharpness in the loss landscape means the model's predictions are fragile—small changes in weights make large changes in recommendations. Tail items, with few training examples, naturally have sharp loss landscapes. By penalizing sharpness, the model learns to be more robust and generalize better to unseen tail items. The item-level design captures fine-grained differences in how popular each item is.
314.po: The method improves recommendation quality for tail items while maintaining head-item performance, and includes a theoretical analysis showing the generalization bound improves faster with the method. This addresses the long-standing practical problem in e-commerce where recommenders systematically ignore niche catalog items.
